title: Deutsch-Jozsa: 2^(n-1)+1 exact classical queries vs 1 exact quantum query (no gap once classical error is allowed)
problem_statement: Given oracle access to f: {0,1}^n -> {0,1} with the promise that f is either constant (all 2^n values equal) or balanced (exactly 2^(n-1) zeros and 2^(n-1) ones), decide which. The answer must be correct with certainty (exact / zero-error setting) for the separation recorded here.

input.parameter: n = number of input bits of f; N = 2^n.
input.size_measure: Query model: cost is the number of oracle calls. The harness materialises the N-entry truth table only so that the oracle can be simulated.

algorithms.name: classical deterministic: scan until a difference or a majority
algorithms.idea: Query x = 0, 1, 2, ... in a fixed order; answer 'balanced' at the first value different from f(0), and 'constant' after 2^(n-1) + 1 equal values (more than half the table, which no balanced function can show).
algorithms.pseudocode: v = f(0); for x in 1..2^(n-1): if f(x) != v: return balanced; return constant
algorithms.time_complexity: 2^(n-1) + 1 queries in the worst case (optimal for exact classical algorithms); about 3 queries on average over uniformly random balanced functions
algorithms.correctness: If two values differ, f is not constant, so by the promise it is balanced. If 2^(n-1) + 1 values agree, f has more than 2^(n-1) equal values, so it is not balanced, hence constant. Never wrong.

algorithms.name: classical randomized, one-sided bounded error (K = 20 random queries)
algorithms.idea: Query K = 20 uniformly random points; answer 'balanced' if two answers differ (certainly right), else 'constant'. Wrong only on balanced functions, with probability exactly 2^(1-K).
algorithms.pseudocode: S = {f(r_1), ..., f(r_K)} for independent uniform r_i; return balanced if |S| = 2 else constant
algorithms.time_complexity: K = 20 queries for every n: O(1); O(log(1/eps)) queries for error probability eps
algorithms.correctness: Constant f always gives |S| = 1. For balanced f each answer is an independent fair bit, so all K agree with probability 2 * 2^(-K) = 2^(1-K) (here 2^-19). Elementary.

algorithms.name: Deutsch-Jozsa quantum algorithm (one-query version)
algorithms.idea: Hadamard transform, one phase-oracle query, Hadamard transform, measure. The amplitude of |0...0> is (1/N) sum_x (-1)^f(x): +-1 if f is constant and exactly 0 if f is balanced.
algorithms.pseudocode: H^n |0>; apply |x> -> (-1)^f(x) |x>; H^n; measure; return constant iff outcome = 0
algorithms.time_complexity: 1 query, exact (zero error); O(n) gates besides the oracle
algorithms.correctness: Deutsch & Jozsa 1992 (original, two-query version); one-query version in Cleve, Ekert, Macchiavello & Mosca 1998. The final amplitude on |0...0> is (1/N) sum_x (-1)^f(x), which is +-1 or 0 under the promise, so the outcome decides with certainty.

lower_bounds.bound: 2^(n-1) + 1 queries in the worst case, for any algorithm that is always correct
lower_bounds.setting: query (oracle) model, EXACT (zero-error) computation, unconditional. The same argument forces 2^(n-1) + 1 queries on every constant input for zero-error randomized (Las Vegas) algorithms. It does NOT hold for bounded-error randomized algorithms, which need only O(1) queries (see the randomized algorithm in this entry).
lower_bounds.source: Elementary adversary argument: answer f(x) = 0 to the first 2^(n-1) distinct queries; both the constant-0 function and a balanced function (ones on unqueried points only) remain consistent, so no exact algorithm can stop. Spelled out in this entry's correctness fields and README; the comparison with exact deterministic computation goes back to Deutsch & Jozsa 1992.

relationship: EXACT setting: 1 quantum query vs 2^(n-1) + 1 classical queries (deterministic, and also any zero-error randomized algorithm on constant inputs), an exponential separation in the query model. BOUNDED-ERROR setting: a classical randomized algorithm needs only O(log(1/eps)) = O(1) queries, so there is no asymptotic separation. Deutsch-Jozsa is therefore evidence for quantum advantage only against exact (zero-error) classical computation; Bernstein-Vazirani and Simon's problem were the next steps toward separations that survive classical randomness (see simon-classical-vs-quantum).

sources.title: Rapid solution of problems by quantum computation
sources.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A 439(1907), 553-558

sources.title: Quantum algorithms revisited

verification.method: V1: all three algorithms agree on the answer, which an independent check confirms by counting the ones in the full truth table, on random constant and random balanced functions for n = 1..16 (quantum simulated exactly with lib/qsim.py up to n = 10). The randomized algorithm can err (probability 2^-19 per balanced instance), so its V1 agreement is itself a probabilistic statement. V2 measures QUERY COUNTS reported through lib.qsim.Oracle. The deterministic algorithm is measured on harness.generate_scaling, the worst-case inputs for its fixed query order (both constants and f(x) = c XOR top bit); there its count is exactly 2^(n-1) + 1, so the fit against that expression is exact (alpha = 1.000). The quantum algorithm uses exactly 1 query and the randomized one exactly 20 for every n (constant-cost checks, max/min = 1.000). experiments/2026-10-07_deutsch_jozsa_checks.py verifies by exhaustion over all promise inputs for n = 1..4 that the maximum of the deterministic count is 2^(n-1) + 1 and is attained on exactly those four inputs, that the simulated quantum algorithm's P(outcome 0) is 1 or 0 to within 3.1e-15, and that the randomized error rate matches 2^(1-k) (|z| <= 0.98 for k = 2..8).

caveats: The exponential gap holds ONLY against exact classical algorithms: with any constant error probability a classical randomized algorithm uses O(1) queries, so Deutsch-Jozsa gives no separation between bounded-error classical and quantum query complexity. It is a promise (partial-function) problem, and a separation relative to an oracle; it does not imply BQP != BPP (it does not even separate the bounded-error query complexities). The V2 fit of the deterministic algorithm uses its worst-case inputs; on random balanced inputs it stops after about 3 queries.
notes: Historically the first problem for which a quantum algorithm was shown to beat every exact classical algorithm exponentially. The original 1992 algorithm used two queries; the one-query, zero-error form implemented here is from Cleve, Ekert, Macchiavello & Mosca 1998 (attribution per secondary sources; the 1992 paper's text could not be accessed for this entry, so no detail of its wording is relied on). The lower bound recorded here is proven in the entry itself and does not depend on that attribution.
